CASE REPORT
Paraneoplastic Stiff Person Syndrome Secondary
to Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
A 70-year-old previously healthy female presented with sudden-onset right lower limb stiffness and pain for 5 days.
On the last follow-up, 23 months after her Whipple surgery, she is still alive and well at the time of writing.
A 70-year-old previously healthy female presented with sudden-onset right lower limb stiffness and pain for 5 days.

A search for an underlying neoplasm was performed via computed tomography (CT) of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis revealing a 1-cm hypodense tumour in the uncinate process of the pancreas suspicious for a pancreatic adenocarcinoma (Fig. 1). A mediastinal mass consistent with a thymoma was also detected. This was initially thought to be the cause of the SPS.

A Whipple procedure was performed and final histology revealed a moderately differentiated 1. 5-cm adenocarcinoma with clear margins and negative lymph nodes. She had an uneventful postoperative course and received adjuvant chemotherapy. Postoperatively, she surprisingly experienced a significant clinical improvement in her symptoms leading us to believe her SPS symptoms to be due to paraneoplastic syndrome secondary to pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

A 70-year-old previously healthy female presented with sudden-onset right lower limb stiffness and pain for 5 days.

Neurological examination revealed isolated right lower limb weakness with Medical Research Council Scale for Muscle Strength 3/5. There was terminal neck stiffness hypertonia in all four limbs. Sensation to pinprick and proprioception were intact. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ in the upper and lower extremities, with severe spasticity resulting in inability to elicit ankle clonus.

Interestingly, the patient presented with a recurrence of SPS 15 months after pancreatectomy. Laboratory and CT scan then did not reveal any tumour recurrence. However, subsequent follow-up scans 3 months later revealed development of metastatic adenopathy anterior to the distal coeliac trunk consistent with local recurrence of her pancreatic cancer (Fig. 2). As there was no evidence of distal metastasis, this further corroborated the proposed link between pancreatic neoplasm and SPS in this patient. Not only did her symptoms resolve after pancreatectomy but the recurrence of her SPS did in fact precede clinically detectable cancer recurrence by several months.

Her case was subsequently reviewed at a multidisciplinary tumour board and the recurrent disease was deemed unresectable and not suitable for debulking as the tumour encased the mesenteric vessels. She has since been started on palliative chemotherapy and her SPS symptoms have been managed symptomatically together with neurologic physiotherapy. On the last follow-up, 23 months after her Whipple surgery, she is still alive and well at the time of writing.

These criteria were all fulfilled by this patient.

�� Stiffness in the axial muscles, especially in the abdominal and thoracolumbar paraspinal muscles leading to a fixed deformity typically hyperlordosis
�� Superimposed painful spasms triggered by emotional stress, tactile stimuli, sudden noises
�� Electromyography confirmation of continuous motor unit activity simultaneously occurring in both agonist and antagonist muscles
�� Absence of other neurologic or cognitive disease causing the stiffness/rigidity
�� Positive serology for GAD65 (or amphiphysin) autoantibodies by immunocytochemistry, western blot or radioimmunoassay
�� Response to diazepam

To our knowledge, there have only been sporadic instances of neuroendocrine pancreatic cancers reported to produce paraneoplastic SPS.
6 This report highlights the first documented instance of pancreatic adenocarcinoma presenting with paraneoplastic SPS. To note, the Dalakas criteria is one of the available guidelines referred to for diagnosing SPS (Table 1). 3 Diagnostic features are based on clinical symptoms, EMG findings supportive of continuous motor activity at rest and serology testing positive for GAD65 autoantibodies, or other forms of autoantibodies. 7 These criteria were all fulfilled by this patient.
